On a PDE-ODE-PDE model for two interacting cell populations under the influence of an acidic environment and with nonlocal intra- and interspecific growth limitation

Maria Eckardt Note: eckardt@mathematik.uni-kl.de    and    Christina Surulescu Note: surulescu@mathematik.uni-kl.de Affiliation: RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau, Felix-Klein-Zentrum für Mathematik, Affiliation: Paul-Ehrlich-Str. 31, 67663 Kaiserslautern, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We consider a model for the dynamics of active cells interacting with their quiescent counterparts under the influence of acidity characterized by proton concentration. The active cells perform nonlinear diffusion and infer proliferation or decay, according to the strength of spatially nonlocal intra- and interspecific interactions. The two cell phenotypes are interchangeable, the transitions depending on the environmental acidity. We prove global existence of a weak solution to the considered PDE-ODE-PDE system and perform numerical simulations in 1D to informally investigate boundedness and patterning behavior in dependence of the system’s parameters and kernels involved in the nonlocal terms.

1 Introduction

Tumor heterogeneity is a well established fact [23]. The neoplastic tissue is -among others- composed of several cell phenotypes, all of which are related to the stage within the cell cycle. To simply, of this vast variety we only consider here two phenotypes: active and quiescent cells. The former are supposed to be motile and proliferate, while the latter just infer transitions toward or from activity. While competing with their active counterparts, quiescent cells can also be degraded. Furthermore, the advancement through the cell cycle and the corresponding phenotypic switch is influenced, inter alia, by biochemical factors in the peritumoral space, see [23] and references therein. In particular, pH regulation is a key feature in tumor cell cycle progression, which it can delay or even inhibit [4, 20, 19, 37].

The interactions of cells with their environment occur not only locally, but cells can percieve their surroundings in a far more extensive manner, by way of protrusions like cytonemes/filopodia/invadopodia, tunneling nanotubes etc. [9, 38, 42, 33]. This motivated the introduction of mathematical models for cell migration, proliferation, and spread. Most of them are of the reaction-diffusion-transport type, with spatial nonlocalities occuring in the advection terms, mainly to model cell-cell and/or cell-tissue adhesions, or nonlocal taxis see e.g. [2, 25, 14, 35, 12, 43, 8, 16], or in the source terms, to describe intraspecific interactions over a whole sensing range [28, 15]. We refer to e.g., [1, 39, 34] for settings also involving nonlocal interspecific competition in different, but related contexts, where the focus is on global stability and pattern issues. The work [40] also considered spatially nonlocal interspecific interactions, but of cancer cells with extracellular matrix and both species featured such terms. For a recent review on nonlocal models for cell migration see [10]; for more comprehensive reviews of nonlocal models in a broader context refer to [17, 26].

Nonlocal models can be obtained, thus far still in a non-rigorous manner, from space- or velocity-jump descriptions on the mesoscopic level (also including the kinetic theory of active particles framework [3]), possibly also accounting for microscale dynamics like binding of transmembrane units to soluble or unsoluble ligands. We refer to [43, 28, 15, 13, 6] for such deductions.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: in Section 2 we present the model consisting of a PDE-ODE-PDE system, along with requirements for the involved parameters and functions. Sections 3 and 4 are dedicated to proving global existence of a nonnegative weak solution to the system, in the sense specified therein. In Section 5 we perform numerical simulations in 1D within various scenarios, to get some insight into boundedness and patterning behavior under the influence of different choices of relevant parameters, interaction kernels, and phenotypic switch triggered by acidity. Finally, Section 6 provides some concluding remarks and an outlook. The appendix Sections A and B contain several auxiliary results needed for the proofs in Section 3.

2 Model

In the following uu and ww represent the densities of active and of quiescent cells, respectively, whereas hh is the concentration of protons in the extracellular space. By ’active’ we mean here cells which are migrating and proliferating. On the other hand, ’quiescent’ means cells which only interact with their active counterparts and with the environment, without moving nor being able to proliferate. We consider the IBVP within a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} having a sufficiently regular boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega and with no-flux boundary conditions

{∂tu=∇⋅(ψ(w,h)∇u)+μ1uα(1−J1(x,h)∗uβ−J2(x,h)∗wγ)+μ~3(h)F(w),x∈Ω,t>0,∂tw=μ2​(h)​(1−w)​u−μ3​(h)​F​(w),x∈Ω,t>0,∂th=DH​Δ​h+g⁡(u,w)−λ​h,x∈Ω,t>0∂νu=∂νh=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0u(x,0)=u0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),h(x,0)=h0(x),x∈Ω.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\nabla\cdot\left(\psi(w,h)\nabla u\right)+\mu_{1}u^{\alpha}\left(1-J_{1}(x,h)\ast u^{\beta}-J_{2}(x,h)\ast w^{\gamma}\right)+\tilde{\mu}_{3}(h)F(w),&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \partial_{t}w=\mu_{2}(h)(1-w)u-\mu_{3}(h){F(w)},&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \partial_{t}h=D_{H}\Delta h+g(u,w)-\lambda h,&x\in\Omega,t>0\\ \partial_{\nu}u=\partial_{\nu}h=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\,w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),\,h(x,0)=h_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega.\end{cases} (2.1)

The first term on the right hand side of the first PDE in (2.1) describes nonlinear diffusion of active cells. The diffusion coefficient ψ\psi can thereby depend on ww and hh: a large amount of ww-cells can increase the population pressure, thus leading to faster diffusion; too many quiescent cells would, however, impede migration (e.g., due to lack of space). Large hh-values are also supposed to enhance motility, as the active cells tend to leave such areas faster than more favorable places. The next term describes proliferation of active cells, which is limited by spatially nonlocal intra- and interspecific interactions. As in previous works [28, 15] we consider the exponents α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma in the weak Allee effect and the competition/crowding terms with the interaction kernels J1J_{1} and J2J_{2}. The latter can be seen as weighting the influence of either interactions on the dynamics of uu over a whole region. This description enables a more flexible characterization of the interaction strengths and is related to the size of uu- and w−w-cell clusters exchanging information with (bunches of) active cells. Eventually, the last term describes phenotypic switch from quiescent to active cells; this transition is happening with a certain saturation and its rate μ~3\tilde{\mu}_{3} depends on the concentration hh of protons. Indeed, less acidic environments favor exit from the quiescent phase and advancement towards activity [41, 7].

The second equation in (2.1) is an ODE describing the dynamics of quiescent cells. These are supposed to be non-motile, to be produced by active cells with a rate μ2\mu_{2} which depends on the acidity in the peritumoral space, and to infer a transition to activity, again with an acidity-dependent rate μ3\mu_{3}, which might differ from μ~3\tilde{\mu}_{3}. We also include a kind of acidity-triggered competition between active and quiescent cells; it might have an own rate, but to keep the number of model coefficients as low as possible we take it to be μ2​(h)\mu_{2}(h), too.

The third equation in system (2.1) is again a reaction-diffusion PDE and models the dynamics of proton concentration hh. Protons are very small in comparison with cells and accordingly able to diffuse quite fastly. They are produced by both tumor cell phenotypes (primarily by active cells and to a lesser amount by quiescent ones) and infer natural decay (e.g., by proton buffering).

Concrete choices of motility, transition, and proliferation coefficients will be provided in Section 5. We define the convolution over Ω\Omega for an hh-dependent kernel as

(J⁡(⋅,h)∗u)​(x)=∫ΩJ⁡(x−y,h⁡(y))​u​(y)​d​y.\displaystyle\left(J(\cdot,h)\ast u\right)(x)=\int_{\Omega}J(x-y,h(y))u(y)\text{d}y. (2.2)

This setting extends our macroscopic model from [15] in the sense that we consider here two interacting populations, the dynamics of both being influenced by that of the acidity in their surroundings. Instead of the tumor diffusion tensor depending only on space we have here a dependency on two of the solution components, however we do not include any repellent pH-taxis, but focus instead on the nonlocal interactions and on the phenotypic switch. It also extends the model in [40], where the two interacting species are not influenced by a third one, the diffusion of cells is of the linear type, and there are no transitions from one species to the other, although all interactions therein are nonlocal in space.

The model can be obtained in a way similar to the meso-to-macro deduction performed in [15], if the dynamics of ww and hh is given as in the second and third equations of (2.1), respectively. Although it is not clear how to obtain nonlinear diffusion in general, this can be achieved if the diffusion coefficient is only depending on macroscopic quantities other than uu. If only linear diffusion is considered, then the method provides a space-dependent (myopic) diffusion tensor of uu-cells, which by an adequate choice of the cell velocity distribution leads to classical Fickian diffusion.

Furthermore, CiC_{i}, i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, denotes by convention a positive constant or a positive function of its arguments.

These assumptions are primarily made out of technical reasons, in order to support the analysis in Subsections 3 and 4, however most of them are reasonable from the application viewpoint: all parameters should be nonnegative and the interactions should involve at least one cell on either side; the diffusion of active and motile cells should be nondegenerate; there should be an effective, but uniformly limited production of protons, which should not dominate the natural decay in a too substantial manner; the interaction kernels should be nonnegative and there should be genuine intraspecific interactions, while the proton concentration remains reasonably bounded, and the initial conditions should be nonnegative and uniformly bounded.

5 1D Simulations

In this section we simulate the behavior of solutions to (2.1) in one dimension. Thereby, we decompose the domain Ω=[−5,5]\Omega=[-5,5] into an equidistant mesh x2,…,xN−1x_{2},\dots,x_{N-1} with step size d​x=0.05dx=0.05 and the time interval [0,50][0,50] with step size d​t=0.0001dt=0.0001. For a simulation of the no-flux boundary condition we add points x1<x2x_{1}<x_{2} and xN>xN−1x_{N}>x_{N-1} outside of Ω\Omega and assume equality of the solutions on the neighboring points. As in [15], we use the method from [32] to discretize the nonlocal integral terms via a composite trapezoidal rule. Moreover, as in [43], we recompute the convolution matrices only every 40 times steps to improve the runtime. Thereby, we assume that changes in the values of the convolution matrices p​h​i​_​m​a​t1phi\_mat_{1} and p​h​i​_​m​a​t2phi\_mat_{2} (due to changes of hh) are negligible within this time interval. Namely, for i,j∈{2,…,N−1}i,j\in\{2,\dots,N-1\} the corresponding entry of the kkth-convolution matrix is

(p​h​i​_​m​a​t1)i​jk=J1​(xi−xj,hj40​k).\displaystyle(phi\_mat_{1})_{ij}^{k}=J_{1}(x_{i}-x_{j},h_{j}^{40k}).

and with the help of this we compute the n+1n+1st convolution term at xix_{i}, i∈{2,…,N−1}i\in\{2,\dots,N-1\} as:

(c​o​n​v1)in+1=∑j=3N−2(p​h​i​_​m​a​t1)i​j⌊n/40⌋​(ujn)β+12​((p​h​i​_​m​a​t1)i​2⌊n/40⌋​(u2n)β+(p​h​i​_​m​a​t1)i⁡(N−1)⌊n/40⌋​(u2n)β)\displaystyle(conv_{1})_{i}^{n+1}=\sum_{j=3}^{N-2}(phi\_mat_{1})_{ij}^{\lfloor n/40\rfloor}(u_{j}^{n})^{\beta}+\frac{1}{2}\left((phi\_mat_{1})_{i2}^{\lfloor n/40\rfloor}(u_{2}^{n})^{\beta}+(phi\_mat_{1})_{i(N-1)}^{\lfloor n/40\rfloor}(u_{2}^{n})^{\beta}\right)

Analogously we compute p​h​i​_​m​a​t2phi\_mat_{2} and c​o​n​v2conv_{2}. For the discretization of the diffusion term we use finite differences and an upwind scheme. The initial conditions are depicted in Figure 1 and are given by

u0​(x)\displaystyle u_{0}(x) ={0.3​e−15​(x+5)2,x∈[−5,0],0.3​e−5​(1−x5),x∈(0,5],,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0.3e^{-\frac{1}{5}(x+5)^{2}},&x\in[-5,0],\\ 0.3e^{-5}\left(1-\frac{x}{5}\right),&x\in(0,5],\end{cases},
w0​(x)\displaystyle w_{0}(x) ={0.7​e−(x+5)2,x∈[−5,0],0.7​e−25​(1−x5),x∈(0,5],,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0.7e^{-(x+5)^{2}},&x\in[-5,0],\\ 0.7e^{-25}\left(1-\frac{x}{5}\right),&x\in(0,5],\end{cases},
h0​(x)\displaystyle h_{0}(x) ={0.3​e−5,x∈[−5,0],0.3​e−5​(1−x5),x∈(0,5],.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0.3e^{-5},&x\in[-5,0],\\ 0.3e^{-5}\left(1-\frac{x}{5}\right),&x\in(0,5],\end{cases}.

We choose the functions ψ⁡(h,w)=0.5\psi(h,w)=0.5 (for simplicity), μ2​(h)=h\mu_{2}(h)=h (meaning that the net ’deactivation’ of uu-cells is directly proportional to the amount of protons available in the microtumor space), μ3​(h)=μ~3​(h)=h1+h\mu_{3}(h)=\tilde{\mu}_{3}(h)=\frac{h}{1+h} (there is no loss of ww-cells when becoming uu-cells, the transition - primarily to motility- is favored by acidity, but in a limited manner, quickly reaching saturation), g⁡(u,w)=u+w1+u+wg(u,w)=\frac{u+w}{1+u+w} (both phenotypes are producing acid, also in a limited way), and the constants DH=0.1D_{H}=0.1 and λ=1\lambda=1.

First, we took β=γ=μ1=1\beta=\gamma=\mu_{1}=1 and explored the influence of the kernels on the minimal value α∗\alpha^{*} of α\alpha for which the solution ceases to exist globally in time (with accuracy to one decimal place). Thereby, we considered as in [15] the logistic kernel JL​(x)=12+ex+e−xJ_{L}(x)=\frac{1}{2+e^{x}+e^{-x}}, the uniform kernel JU​(x)=χ[−1,1]​(x)J_{U}(x)=\chi_{[-1,1]}(x) and, moreover, the hh-dependent kernels

J1​(x,h)\displaystyle J_{1}(x,h) =12​π​e−x22​(h1+h+110),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}\left(\frac{h}{1+h}+\frac{1}{10}\right), (5.1)
J2​(x,h)\displaystyle J_{2}(x,h) =h22​(1+h2),\displaystyle=\frac{h^{2}}{2(1+h^{2})}, (5.2)

the first of which is a hh- dependent shift of a Gaussian, while the latter is a Holling III-type function of hh suggesting a slower increase towards saturation, with a certain ’learning effect’ as far as the response to more acidity is concerned: as J2J_{2} stands for the interaction of the two cell phenotypes, it accounts for both of them extruding protons, along with the corresponding adaptation of uu-cells to interspecific cues.

The first columns of Figures 2 and 3 show the solution for the critical α\alpha from (2.3), when J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} are both logistic or uniform, respectively. The solution uu aggregates at the position of the initial accumulation of the active cells at the left boundary. In the case of two logistic kernels a stronger aggregation for increasing α\alpha values can be observed leading to a blow-up at the left boundary near α∗=6.2\alpha^{*}=6.2. On the other hand, in the case of two uniform kernels uu invades the whole domain and aggregates at the right boundary, leading to a blow-up there for approximately α∗=14.7\alpha^{*}=14.7. This invasive behavior can also be observed for all combinations of kernels and parameters α,β,γ,μ\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\mu as long as no blow-up at the left boundary occurs. An overview of the minimal values α∗\alpha^{*} depending on the kernels can be found in Table 1.

In further tests we investigated for logistic kernels the influence of β\beta,γ\gamma and the growth rate μ1\mu_{1} on the blow-up behavior. Higher values of β\beta lead to an increase of the minimal value α∗\alpha^{*} where blow-up occurs. In the case β=10\beta=10 and γ=μ1=1\gamma=\mu_{1}=1 we observed that for α=26.9,27.1,27.3\alpha=26.9,27.1,27.3 the solution ceases to exist, whereas it exists globally in time for α=27,27.2,27.4\alpha=27,27.2,27.4. Hence, in contrast to [15, 28] we cannot determine a value α∗\alpha^{*} s.t. for α<α∗\alpha<\alpha^{*} the solution is global, whereas it blows-up for α≥α∗\alpha\geq\alpha^{*}. It seems that for α≥α∗⁣∗=27.5\alpha\geq\alpha^{**}=27.5 blow-up occurs but we cannot assure this. In contrast, higher values of γ\gamma and/or μ\mu lead to a blow-up for lower α\alpha’s, see Table 2 for an overview of the concrete values of α∗\alpha^{*} along with the respective parameter combinations.

Moreover, as in [15], increasing values of β\beta and μ1\mu_{1} in Figure 4 lead to patterns depending on the kernels J1J_{1} and J2J_{2}. A high value of γ\gamma does not seem to lead by itself to patterns, but further experiments suggest that γ\gamma influences the height of the peaks, thus leading to less pronounced uu-patterns. This is due to the stronger dampening of proliferation, which hinders stronger aggregates. To illustrate the effect of γ\gamma we plot in Figure 4 two situations with very different values (γ=1000\gamma=1000 in the first column and γ=1\gamma=1 in the remaining columns).

The performed simulations are very similar to those of the reduced model

{∂tu=∇⋅(ψ(h)∇u)+μ1uα(1−J(x,h)∗uβ),x∈Ω,t>0,∂th=DH​Δ​h+g⁡(u)−λ​h,x∈Ω,t>0\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\nabla\cdot\left(\psi(h)\nabla u\right)+\mu_{1}u^{\alpha}\left(1-J(x,h)\ast u^{\beta}\right),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \partial_{t}h=D_{H}\Delta h+g(u)-\lambda h,&x\in\Omega,\ t>0\end{cases} (5.3)

without inactive cells ww (compare rows 1 and 2 and rows 3 and 4 in Figure 4, respectively, for uniform or logistic kernels). System (5.3) is a simplification of the model considered in [15] without myopic diffusion and taxis, where Turing-like patterns for large values of β​μ1\beta\mu_{1} were induced by the nonlocal term. This also seems to be the case here in model (2.1). However, the calculation of a strictly positive steady-state (u∗,w∗,h∗)(u^{*},w^{*},h^{*}) already leads to analytical problems, since this requires even in the corresponding local model without diffusion and for μ2,μ3,μ~3\mu_{2},\mu_{3},\tilde{\mu}_{3} independent from hh a solution to the nonlinear system

0\displaystyle 0 =μ1​(u∗)α​(1−(u∗)β−(w∗)γ)+μ~3​w∗1+w∗,\displaystyle=\mu_{1}\left(u^{*}\right)^{\alpha}\left(1-\left(u^{*}\right)^{\beta}-\left(w^{*}\right)^{\gamma}\right)+\tilde{\mu}_{3}\frac{w^{*}}{1+w^{*}},
0\displaystyle 0 =μ2​(1−w∗)​u∗−μ3​w∗1+w∗.\displaystyle=\mu_{2}(1-w^{*})u^{*}-\mu_{3}\frac{w^{*}}{1+w^{*}}.

Comparing the height of the peaks in columns 3 and 4 of Figure 4 for uniform kernels (i.e., first two rows therein) clearly shows the dampening effect of interspecific interactions. Moreover, the solution of (5.3) reaches its maximum accumulation at the left boundary faster than the solution of (2.1), which is again due to the supplementary interspecific dampening in the latter model. Figure 5 shows that in model (5.3) a blow-up already occurs for relatively smaller values of α\alpha.

For the hh-dependent kernels J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} from (5.1) and (5.2) the solution uu in Figure 6 rapidly accumulates at the left boundary and then invades the whole domain aggregating much less at the boundaries than in Figures 2 and 3. As mentioned in Table 1 the blow-up already occurs for α∗=4.1\alpha^{*}=4.1. The 4th column in Figure 6 shows one example of pattern formation for a certain choice of parameters.

6 Discussion

As mentioned in Section 2, the model introduced here extends previous settings [28] and, in a certain sense, [15, 40]. As in [28, 15], the main mathematical challenge comes from the interaction strengths α,β≥1\alpha,\beta\geq 1 present in the nonlocal terms; interspecific interactions did not add further difficulties as far as global existence and boundedness are concerned. In contrast to [15] we do not have here any myopic diffusion, nor taxis terms, which saves us the efforts otherwise needed to estimate first derivatives of the tactic signal. The model with interspecific interactions from [40] involves haptotaxis, but there α=β=γ=1\alpha=\beta=\gamma=1 and the lack of transitions from one population to another, along with the assumptions made on initial data, convolution kernels, and coefficient functions render the analysis therein more accessible.

The missing diffusion of ww-cells required the construction of the approximate problem in Section 3. Introducing the term −w​u-wu in the dynamics of ww-cells helped ensure in that problem the boundedness of wεw_{\varepsilon}, with the aid of a comparison principle. Such term does have a biological motivation as well: it describes competition between active and inactive cells, which in our model is also triggered by the acidity profile, as both tumor cell phenotypes extrude protons in the interstitial space (the active ones more than their quiescent counterparts).

As in [28, 15], the condition (2.3) is not sharp: the numerical simulations suggest that the solution also exists globally for certain pairs (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) which do not satisfy that requirement. Interestingly, the critical value α∗\alpha^{*} for which a solution ceases to exist does not seem to be an absolute α\alpha-minimum, but can jump to higher or lower values, depending on the particular combination of the other parameters β,γ,μ1\beta,\gamma,\mu_{1} (even for the same choice of kernels), as seen in Table 2. Indeed, there seems to be an α∗⁣∗>α∗\alpha^{**}>\alpha^{*} such that the solution blows up in finite time for α≥α∗⁣∗\alpha\geq\alpha^{**}, but stays global for certain values α∈(α∗,α∗⁣∗)\alpha\in(\alpha^{*},\alpha^{**}). A thorough mathematical investigation thereof remains, however, open. As Table 1 shows, α∗\alpha^{*} also depends on the choice of convolution kernels (for fixed parameter values); this greatly complicates the analysis of blow-up behavior, due to the unlimited degrees of freedom one has for such choices, notwithstanding conditions (2.6).

A rigorous mathematical stability and pattern analysis for this kind of PDE-ODE-PDE models seems to be out of reach with the established approaches (see, e.g., [1, 34, 30, 39]), mainly due to the nonlinearities featuring weak Allee and overcrowding/competition effects with the respective interaction strengths α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma, which preclude from identifying nontrivial steady-states even in the absence of diffusion; the phenotypic switch terms only add difficulty to such attempts. The numerical simulations performed in Section 5 give some insight into the long-term and patterning behavior of solutions, suggesting that the solution seems to be able to approach in the long term some stable state and to exhibit patterns, depending (as in [15]) on the choice of kernels and the parameter combination. The model extension with ww-cells and interspecific interactions does not change substantially the type and shape of obtained oscillatory patterns, but does have an influence on the peaks of uu-cell aggregates. The noticed dampening effect also contributes to detering solution blow-up or at least ensuring global boundedness for substantially larger α\alpha values which, again, depend on the choice of the convolution kernels and of the interaction strength γ\gamma.

Our analysis explicitly required the diffusion coefficient ψ⁡(w,h)\psi(w,h) to be nondegenerate. Alleviating this assumption leads to further mathematical challenges, when trying to obtain (as usually in such proofs) a bound on ∇u\nabla u from the ODE for ww. Indeed, the problem thereby relies on uu being involved in the growth, instead of the decay term. On the other hand, considering such nonlinear diffusion is motivated from a biological viewpoint, in order to account e.g., for chemokinesis [21, 24, 36].

    ‖u−u⁡(⋅,0)‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T])+⟨u−u⁡(⋅,0)⟩x,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ\displaystyle\|u-u(\cdot,0)\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}+\langle u-u(\cdot,0)\rangle_{x,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\vartheta}
    ≤\displaystyle\leq (‖u−u⁡(⋅,0)‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T])+∑i=1d‖uxi−uxi​(⋅,0)‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T]))\displaystyle\left(\|u-u(\cdot,0)\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\|u_{x_{i}}-u_{x_{i}}(\cdot,0)\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}\right)
    ≤\displaystyle\leq \Cr​e​i​n​b​s​o​b​2​(T1+ϑ2​⟨u⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]1+ϑ2+Tϑ2​∑i=1d⟨uxi⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ2)\displaystyle\Cr{einbsob2}\left(T^{\frac{1+\vartheta}{2}}\langle u\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{1+\vartheta}{2}}+T^{\frac{\vartheta}{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\langle u_{x_{i}}\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{\vartheta}{2}}\right) (A.5)

    Putting this together with the supremum of (A.4) and performing a similar calcution with the terms in (A.5) we obtain (A.1) due to T<1T<1.

  2. 2.

    Let u∈C2+ϑ,1+ϑ2​(Ω¯×[0,T])u\in C^{2+\vartheta,1+\frac{\vartheta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]). Let t,t′∈[0,T]t,t^{\prime}\in[0,T], t≠t′t\neq t^{\prime}, x∈o​ax\in oa. First, we conclude from the mean value theorem that

    ‖u⁡(x,t)−u⁡(x,0)‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T])+⟨u−u⁡(x,0)⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]1+ϑ2≤(T+T1−ϑ2)​‖ut‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T]).\displaystyle\|u(x,t)-u(x,0)\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}+\langle u-u(x,0)\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{1+\vartheta}{2}}\leq(T+T^{\frac{1-\vartheta}{2}})\|u_{t}\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}.

    Moreover,

    ⟨uxi−uxi​(⋅,0)⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ2≤Tα2​⟨uxi⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]1+ϑ2\displaystyle\langle u_{x_{i}}-u_{x_{i}}(\cdot,0)\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{\vartheta}{2}}\leq T^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\langle u_{x_{i}}\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{1+\vartheta}{2}}

    As in (A.5) we use the continuous embedding of W1,∞​(Ω)W^{1,\infty}(\Omega) into Cϑ​(Ω¯)C^{\vartheta}(\overline{\Omega}) (see Theorem ?? in [18]) to estimate

    ‖uxi−uxi​(⋅,0)‖C​Ω¯×[0,T]+⟨uxi−uxi​(⋅,0)⟩x,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ\displaystyle\|u_{x_{i}}-u_{x_{i}}(\cdot,0)\|_{C{\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}}+\langle u_{x_{i}}-u_{x_{i}}(\cdot,0)\rangle_{x,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\vartheta}
    ≤\displaystyle\leq \Cr​e​i​n​b​s​o​b​2​(‖uxi−uxi​(⋅,0)‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T])+∑j=1d‖uxi​xj−uxi​xj​(⋅,0)‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T])).\displaystyle\Cr{einbsob2}\left(\|u_{x_{i}}-u_{x_{i}}(\cdot,0)\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\|u_{x_{i}x_{j}}-u_{x_{i}x_{j}}(\cdot,0)\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}\right).

    Taking the supremum on the left side of

    |uxi​(x,t)−uxi​(x,0)|=t1+ϑ2​|uxi​(x,t)−uxi​(x,0)|t1+ϑ2≤T1+ϑ2​⟨uxi⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]1+ϑ2\displaystyle|u_{x_{i}}(x,t)-u_{x_{i}}(x,0)|=t^{\frac{1+\vartheta}{2}}\frac{|u_{x_{i}}(x,t)-u_{x_{i}}(x,0)|}{t^{\frac{1+\vartheta}{2}}}\leq T^{\frac{1+\vartheta}{2}}\langle u_{x_{i}}\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{1+\vartheta}{2}}

    and analogously

    |uxi​xj​(x,t)−uxi​xj​(x,0)|≤Tϑ2​⟨uxi​xj⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ2\displaystyle|u_{x_{i}x_{j}}(x,t)-u_{x_{i}x_{j}}(x,0)|\leq T^{\frac{\vartheta}{2}}\langle u_{x_{i}x_{j}}\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{\vartheta}{2}}

    together with the above estimates we obtain (A.2).

  3. 3.

    We estimate as before with the help of the mean value theoren and the Sobolev embedding that

    ⟨u−u⁡(⋅,0)⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ2\displaystyle\langle u-u(\cdot,0)\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{\vartheta}{2}} ≤T1−ϑ2​‖ut‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T]),\displaystyle\leq T^{\frac{1-\vartheta}{2}}\|u_{t}\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])},
    ‖u−u⁡(⋅,0)‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T])+⟨u−u⁡(⋅,0)⟩x,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ\displaystyle\|u-u(\cdot,0)\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}+\langle u-u(\cdot,0)\rangle_{x,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\vartheta} ≤\Cr​e​i​n​b​s​o​b​2​(T​‖ut‖C⁡(Ω¯×[0,T])+T1+κ2​∑i=1d⟨uxi⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]1+κ2).\displaystyle\leq\Cr{einbsob2}\left(T\|u_{t}\|_{C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T])}+T^{\frac{1+\kappa}{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\langle u_{x_{i}}\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{1+\kappa}{2}}\right).

∎

Lemma A.3.

Let T>0T>0, Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with sufficiently smooth boundary, ϑ∈(0,1)\vartheta\in(0,1), β≥1\beta\geq 1 and J⁡(x,h)∗uβ=∫ΩJi​(x−y,h⁡(y))​u​(y)​d​yJ(x,h)\ast u^{\beta}=\int_{\Omega}J_{i}(x-y,h(y))u(y)\text{d}y and satisfying

|J⁡(x,h1)−J⁡(x,h2)|≤L⁡(x)​|h1−h2|,\displaystyle|J(x,h_{1})-J(x,h_{2})|\leq L(x)|h_{1}-h_{2}|, (A.6)
L,J⁡(⋅,0)∈Lp​(B)\displaystyle L,\,J(\cdot,0)\in L^{p}(B) (A.7)

for L⁡(⋅)≥0L(\cdot)\geq 0. p∈(1,∞)p\in(1,\infty), h1,h2≥0h_{1},h_{2}\geq 0.

  1. 1.

    If u,h∈L∞​(Ω×(0,T))u,h\in L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T)) then, J⁡(x,h)∗uβ∈L∞​(Ω×(0,T))J(x,h)\ast u^{\beta}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T)) and satisfies

    ‖J⁡(x,h)∗uβ‖L∞​(Ω×(0,T))≤‖u‖L∞​(Ω×(0,T))β​(‖L‖L1​(B)​‖h‖L∞​(Ω×(0,T))+‖J⁡(x,0)‖L1​(B)).\displaystyle\|J(x,h)\ast u^{\beta}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T))}\leq\|u\|^{\beta}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T))}\left(\|L\|_{L^{1}(B)}\|h\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T))}+\|J(x,0)\|_{L^{1}(B)}\right).
  2. 2.

    If u,h∈Cϑ,ϑ2​(Ω¯×[0,T])u,h\in C^{\vartheta,\frac{\vartheta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]) then, J⁡(x,h)∗uβJ(x,h)\ast u^{\beta} is in Cκ,κ2​(Ω¯×[0,T])C^{\kappa,\frac{\kappa}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]) for κ:=min⁡{ϑ,p−1p}\kappa:=\min\{\vartheta,\frac{p-1}{p}\}.

Proof.
  1. 1.

    Let u,h∈L∞​(Ω×(0,T))u,h\in L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T)), x∈Ωx\in\Omega and t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Using (2.6a) and (2.6b) we can estimate

    |J⁡(x,h)∗u⁡(t)|\displaystyle\left|J(x,h)\ast u(t)\right| ≤|∫ΩJ⁡(x−y,h⁡(y,t))​uβ​(y,t)​d​x|\displaystyle\leq\left|\int_{\Omega}J(x-y,h(y,t))u^{\beta}(y,t)\text{d}x\right|
    ≤‖u‖L∞​(Ω×(0,T))β​|∫ΩL⁡(x−y)​|h⁡(y,t)|+|J⁡(x,0)|​d​x|\displaystyle\leq\|u\|^{\beta}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T))}\left|\int_{\Omega}L(x-y)|h(y,t)|+|J(x,0)|\text{d}x\right|
    ≤‖u‖L∞​(Ω×(0,T))β​(‖L‖L1​(B)​‖h‖L∞​(Ω×(0,T))+‖J⁡(x,0)‖L1​(B)).\displaystyle\leq\|u\|^{\beta}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T))}\left(\|L\|_{L^{1}(B)}\|h\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T))}+\|J(x,0)\|_{L^{1}(B)}\right).

    Taking the supremum on the left-hand side, we conclude that J⁡(x,h)∗u¯∈L∞​(Ω×(0,T))J(x,h)\ast\overline{u}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T)).

  2. 2.

    Let u,h∈Cϑ,ϑ2​(Ω¯×[0,T])u,h\in C^{\vartheta,\frac{\vartheta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]). Let x∈Ω¯x\in\overline{\Omega} and t1,t2∈[0,T],t1≠t2t_{1},t_{2}\in[0,T],t_{1}\neq t_{2}. Then, we can estimate using the properties of JJ, the Hölder continuity of uu and hh and the mean value theorem that

    |J⁡(x,h)∗u¯​(t1)−J⁡(x,h)∗u¯​(t2)|\displaystyle|J(x,h)\ast\overline{u}(t_{1})-J(x,h)\ast\overline{u}(t_{2})|
    =\displaystyle= |∫ΩJ⁡(x−y,h⁡(y,t1))​uβ​(y,t1)−J⁡(x−y,h⁡(y,t2))​uβ​(y,t2)​d​y|\displaystyle\left|\int_{\Omega}J(x-y,h(y,t_{1}))u^{\beta}(y,t_{1})-J(x-y,h(y,t_{2}))u^{\beta}(y,t_{2})\text{d}y\right|
    ≤\displaystyle\leq |∫Ω(J⁡(x−y,h⁡(y,t1))−J⁡(x−y,h⁡(y,t2))​uβ​(y,t1))​d​y|+|J⁡(x−y,h⁡(y,t2))​(uβ​(y,t1)−uβ​(y,t2))​d​y|\displaystyle\left|\int_{\Omega}\left(J(x-y,h(y,t_{1}))-J(x-y,h(y,t_{2}))u^{\beta}(y,t_{1})\right)\text{d}y\right|+\left|J(x-y,h(y,t_{2}))\left(u^{\beta}(y,t_{1})-u^{\beta}(y,t_{2})\right)\text{d}y\right|
    ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖u‖L∞​(Ω)β​∫ΩL⁡(x−y)​|h⁡(y,t1)−h⁡(y,t2)|​d​y\displaystyle\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{\beta}\int_{\Omega}L(x-y)|h(y,t_{1})-h(y,t_{2})|\text{d}y
    +β|u|∫ΩL∞​(Ω)β−1⁡(L⁡(x−y)​|h⁡(y,t2)|+J⁡(x−y,0))​|u⁡(y,t1)−u⁡(y,t2)|​d​y\displaystyle+\beta\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{\beta-1}\int_{\Omega}\left(L(x-y)|h(y,t_{2})|+J(x-y,0)\right)|u(y,t_{1})-u(y,t_{2})|\text{d}y
    ≤\displaystyle\leq (‖u‖L∞,‖h‖L∞,‖L‖L1​(B),‖J⁡(⋅,0)‖L1​(B),β)​(⟨h⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ2+⟨u⟩t,Ω¯×[0,T]ϑ2).\displaystyle\left(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}},\|h\|_{L^{\infty}},\|L\|_{L^{1}(B)},\|J(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{1}(B)},\beta\right)\left(\langle h\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{\vartheta}{2}}+\langle u\rangle_{t,\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]}^{\frac{\vartheta}{2}}\right). (A.8)

    Now, let x1,x2∈Ω¯,x1≠x2x_{1},x_{2}\in\overline{\Omega},x_{1}\neq x_{2} and t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Then, we can estimate

    |J⁡(x1,h)∗u¯​(t)−J⁡(x2,h)∗u¯​(t)|\displaystyle|J(x_{1},h)\ast\overline{u}(t)-J(x_{2},h)\ast\overline{u}(t)|
    =\displaystyle= |∫ℝdJ⁡(x1−y,h⁡(y,t))​uβ​(y)​χΩ​(y)−J⁡(x2−y,h⁡(y,t))​uβ​(y)​χΩ​(y)​d​y|\displaystyle\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}J(x_{1}-y,h(y,t))u^{\beta}(y)\chi_{\Omega}(y)-J(x_{2}-y,h(y,t))u^{\beta}(y)\chi_{\Omega}(y)\text{d}y\right|
    =\displaystyle= |∫ℝdJ⁡(z,h⁡(x1−z,t))​uβ​(x1−z)​χΩ​(x1−z)−J⁡(z,h⁡(x2−z,t))​uβ​(x2−z)​χΩ​(x2−z)​d​z|\displaystyle\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}J(z,h(x_{1}-z,t))u^{\beta}(x_{1}-z)\chi_{\Omega}(x_{1}-z)-J(z,h(x_{2}-z,t))u^{\beta}(x_{2}-z)\chi_{\Omega}(x_{2}-z)\text{d}z\right|
    ≤\displaystyle\leq |∫ℝd(J⁡(z,h⁡(x1−z,t))​uβ​(x1−z)−J⁡(z,h⁡(x2−z,t))​uβ​(x2−z))​χΩ​(x1−z)​χΩ​(x2−z)​d​z|\displaystyle\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(J(z,h(x_{1}-z,t))u^{\beta}(x_{1}-z)-J(z,h(x_{2}-z,t))u^{\beta}(x_{2}-z)\right)\chi_{\Omega}(x_{1}-z)\chi_{\Omega}(x_{2}-z)\text{d}z\right| (A.9)
    +∫ℝd|J(z,h(x1−z,t))uβ(x1−z)χΩ(x1−z)(1−χΩ(x2−z))|dy\displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|J(z,h(x_{1}-z,t))u^{\beta}(x_{1}-z)\chi_{\Omega}(x_{1}-z)(1-\chi_{\Omega}(x_{2}-z))\right|\text{d}y (A.10)
    +∫ℝd|J(z,h(x2−z,t))uβ(x2−z)(1−χΩ(x1−z))χΩ(x2−z)|dz.\displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|J(z,h(x_{2}-z,t))u^{\beta}(x_{2}-z)(1-\chi_{\Omega}(x_{1}-z))\chi_{\Omega}(x_{2}-z)\right|\text{d}z. (A.11)

    We can estimate (A.9) analogously to (A.8). To estimate (A.10) we define the sets

    Sx1​x2\displaystyle S_{x_{1}x_{2}} :={z∈ℝd:x1−z∈Ω,x2−z∉Ω},\displaystyle:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x_{1}-z\in\Omega,x_{2}-z\notin\Omega\right\},
    Gx1​x2\displaystyle G_{x_{1}x_{2}} :={z∈ℝd:x1−z∈Ω,dist(x1−z,∂Ω)≤|x1−x2|}.\displaystyle:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x_{1}-z\in\Omega,\text{dist}\left(x_{1}-z,\partial\Omega\right)\leq|x_{1}-x_{2}|\right\}.

    Let z∈Sx1​x2z\in S_{x_{1}x_{2}}. Then, a:=x1−z∈Ωa:=x_{1}-z\in\Omega and x2−z=x2−x1+a∉Ωx_{2}-z=x_{2}-x_{1}+a\notin\Omega. Assume dist​(x1−z,∂Ω)>|x1−x1|\text{dist}\left(x_{1}-z,\partial\Omega\right)>|x_{1}-x_{1}|. Then, B|x1−x2|​(a)¯⊂Ω\overline{B_{|x_{1}-x_{2}|}(a)}\subset\Omega. Hence, a+x2−x1∈Ωa+x_{2}-x_{1}\in\Omega which leads to a contradiction. Consequently, Sx1​x2⊂Gx1​x2S_{x_{1}x_{2}}\subset G_{x_{1}x_{2}} and |Sx1​x2|≤|Gx1​x2|≤CΩ​|x1−x2||S_{x_{1}x_{2}}|\leq|G_{x_{1}x_{2}}|\leq C_{\Omega}|x_{1}-x_{2}| holds for ∂Ω\partial\Omega sufficiently smooth. Then, we can estimate

    |(A.10)|\displaystyle|\eqref{estjhx2}| =|∫Sx1​x2J⁡(z,h⁡(x1−z,t))​uβ​(x1−z)​d​z|\displaystyle=\left|\int_{S_{x_{1}x_{2}}}J(z,h(x_{1}-z,t))u^{\beta}(x_{1}-z)\text{d}z\right|
    ≤‖u‖L∞​(Ω)β​∫Gx1​x2L⁡(z)​h​(x1−z,t)+J⁡(z,0)​d​z\displaystyle\leq\|u\|^{\beta}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\int_{G_{x_{1}x_{2}}}L(z)h(x_{1}-z,t)+J(z,0)\text{d}z
    ≤‖u‖L∞​(Ω)β​max⁡{1,‖h‖L∞​(Ω)β}​(‖L‖Lp​(B)+‖J⁡(⋅,0)‖Lp​(B))​|Gx1​x2|p−1p\displaystyle\leq\|u\|^{\beta}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\max\{1,\|h\|^{\beta}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\}\left(\|L\|_{L^{p}(B)}+\|J(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{p}(B)}\right)|G_{x_{1}x_{2}}|^{\frac{p-1}{p}}
    ≤|x1−x2|p−1p.\displaystyle\leq|x_{1}-x_{2}|^{\frac{p-1}{p}}.

    We can estimate (A.11) analogously. Putting this together with the estimates of the other terms, we conclude J⁡(x,h)∗uβ∈Cκ,κ2​(Ω¯×[0,T])J(x,h)\ast u^{\beta}\in C^{\kappa,\frac{\kappa}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]) for κ:=min⁡{ϑ,p−1p}\kappa:=\min\{\vartheta,\frac{p-1}{p}\}.

∎

Lemma A.4.

Let T>0T>0. If f∈C⁡([0,T],ℝ0+)∩C1​((0,T),ℝ0+)f\in C([0,T];\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+})\cap C^{1}((0,T);\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}) satisfies on (0,T)(0,T) for K1,K2>0K_{1},K_{2}>0 the inequality

f′​(t)+K1​f​(t)≤K1​K2,\displaystyle f^{\prime}(t)+K_{1}f(t)\leq K_{1}K_{2},

then, for t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T) it holds that

f⁡(t)≤K2+f⁡(0).\displaystyle f(t)\leq K_{2}+f(0).
Proof.

Let t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T). We differentiate

(f⁡(t)​eK1​t)′=(f′​(t)+K1​f​(t))​eK1​t≤K1​K2​eK1​t.\displaystyle\left(f(t)e^{K_{1}t}\right)^{\prime}=(f^{\prime}(t)+K_{1}f(t))e^{K_{1}t}\leq K_{1}K_{2}e^{K_{1}t}.

Integrating over [0,t][0,t] we obtain

f⁡(t)​eK1​t≤K1​K2​∫0teK1​s​d​s+f⁡(0)=K2​(eK1​t−1)+f⁡(0).\displaystyle f(t)e^{K_{1}t}\leq K_{1}K_{2}\int_{0}^{t}e^{K_{1}s}\text{d}s+f(0)=K_{2}\left(e^{K_{1}t}-1\right)+f(0).

Consequently,

f⁡(t)≤K2​(1−e−K1​t)+f⁡(0)​eK1​t≤K2+f⁡(0).\displaystyle f(t)\leq K_{2}\left(1-e^{-K_{1}t}\right)+f(0)e^{K_{1}t}\leq K_{2}+f(0).

∎
